title: Pituitary Gland Anatomy
descriptor: Sella Turcica, Anterior & Posterior Lobes, Hypothalamic Link, Hormones, Pituitary Tumours
intro: The pituitary gland is a small endocrine gland at the base of the brain, about the size of a pea. It sits in a bony hollow of the sphenoid bone and is joined to the hypothalamus by a stalk. The anterior lobe makes its own hormones, while the posterior lobe stores and releases hormones made in the hypothalamus. The pituitary is often described as the body's master control gland.

sections.heading: Location and relations
sections.body: The pituitary gland lies within the sella turcica, a midline depression in the sphenoid bone, and the bony walls of the sella turcica surround the fossa at the front, at the back and below. The sphenoid sinus lies below the gland. Its roof is the diaphragma sellae, which separates the gland from the optic chiasm above, with a cerebrospinal-fluid-filled space between them. On each side lies a cavernous sinus, which contains the internal carotid artery and several cranial nerves. The gland has a dual embryonic origin: the anterior lobe is derived from ectoderm, whereas the posterior lobe is neural in origin.

sections.heading: Lobes, stalk and blood supply
sections.body:
The anterior lobe makes its own hormones, but signals from the hypothalamus control their release. The posterior lobe does not make hormones: it houses the axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons and stores and releases into the bloodstream two hypothalamic hormones, oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also called vasopressin. The hypothalamus and the pituitary gland are connected by a stalk, the infundibulum, which contains blood vessels and nerve axons.

Hormones from the hypothalamus reach the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal system, which carries them directly to the anterior lobe without first entering the general circulation. The anterior lobe is supplied mainly by the superior hypophyseal arteries, which arise from the internal carotid artery and run along the stalk, while the posterior lobe is supplied by the inferior hypophyseal arteries, which also arise from the internal carotid artery and pass below the gland.

sections.heading: Hormones and what they control
sections.body:
The anterior lobe makes growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinising hormone (LH) and prolactin. Several of these hormones direct other endocrine glands: TSH controls the release of thyroid hormones from the thyroid gland, and ACTH governs the release of cortisol from the adrenal cortex. FSH and LH are the pituitary's reproductive hormones, prolactin is involved in lactation, and growth hormone acts on growth, including that of muscle and bone.

The posterior lobe releases ADH, which acts on the kidneys to conserve water, and oxytocin, which acts on the uterus and the breast.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: pituitary tumours
sections.body: Pituitary disorders usually involve too much or too little of one hormone, and a tumour is the most common cause, although injuries can also trigger them. Many pituitary tumours cause no symptoms, and nonfunctioning tumours, which do not release extra hormone, often cause none at all; others cause symptoms through their growth or through the hormones they make. Because the optic chiasm lies just above the gland, a tumour that grows upwards can compress it, so people typically notice blurred or lost peripheral vision, and headache is also common.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: hormone excess
sections.body: Tumours that make extra hormone are called functioning tumours, and their effects depend on which hormone is overproduced. Acromegaly, caused by too much growth hormone, is usually due to a non-cancerous tumour (adenoma) in the pituitary gland. Excess growth hormone can also cause joint pain, and snoring or pauses in breathing during sleep. Cushing's disease results from excess ACTH made by the pituitary, most often by an adenoma. Excess ACTH can cause a fatty lump on the back of the neck, easy bruising and bones that break easily. Prolactin-producing tumours can affect menstrual periods and fertility and can cause milk flow in people who are not pregnant or breastfeeding.

sections.heading: Clinical relevance: underactivity, apoplexy and tests
sections.body:
Hypopituitarism is a shortfall in some or all pituitary hormones, and its causes include tumours of the pituitary or hypothalamus, pituitary apoplexy and infections. Pituitary apoplexy is a rare but serious condition in which there is bleeding into the gland or its blood flow is blocked, and it can be life-threatening if untreated. A sudden severe headache or any worsening of vision should be assessed promptly by a clinician.

When a pituitary tumour is suspected, as in acromegaly, a GP refers the person to a specialist, and diagnosis usually involves blood tests and an MRI scan of the brain to look for a tumour. Treatment depends on the type of tumour and may include surgery, radiotherapy or medicines.
